name: Pinkish Brown
lede: Pinkish Brown names a warm, reddish [[brown]] by plain modifier grammar, and the same pairing of words turns up in older writing describing faded dyes and disliked cats, long before the 2010 survey fixed it to one hex.

sections.title: A modifier with older echoes
sections.body:
The name follows the modifier pattern "pinkish" plus the parent hue [[brown]], and our library's only dated record for this exact swatch is the 2010 xkcd color survey [1]. The phrase itself is older in English: one account of dye history describes brazilwood, a tropical hardwood dye, fading to "a dowdy pinkish brown" [2], and a study of color superstition notes that cats of this shade were once disliked in Japan [3]. Neither passage names this precise hue, so the swatch's own coining stays undocumented [1].

The nearest named colors by measured distance are [[cacao-brown]] and [[etruscan-red]], both almost the same shade [4]. [[blast-off-bronze]] is duller; [[clay-pink]] and [[russet-vinaceous]] read almost the same, and [[copper-penny]] runs redder [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive of 23,781 paintings finds a match for this reddish brown in 372 of them, about 1.56 percent, more common than 66 percent of the named colors we track, as photographed [5]. It peaks in the 1400s, at 1.5 times the expected rate (11 of 945 paintings from then), and inside a painting it plays an accent in 70 percent of cases, ranked by lightness rather than raw area [5]. Gilbert Stuart is its most devoted painter here, using it in 7 of 50 works, 6.8 times the baseline for the museums those works come from [5]. It is most over-represented in Indian paintings, at 2.2 times the expected rate [5]. The earliest match is dated 1230; the archive's early centuries are thin, so that date is a floor, not a first [5].
